content:
"In 2005, author Jeffrey Eugenides said something about American society that feels even more relevant today. He said that as a person gets to know their country better, they discover more things to be ashamed of. This quote is part of a story he wrote called 'Great Experiment' which is part of his first book of short stories 'Fresh Complaint'. Now, more than a decade later, he finds this observation to be more true than ever.

* He mentions that there's a mutual relationship between national shame and personal shame, as they are connected in many ways.
* According to him, every individual has things in their past that they regret, just as every nation does, and this can cause both personal and national shame.

Eugenides suggests that even as we pay attention to the troubling events happening nationally, we should not ignore the personal issues that also bother us. Our problems as a nation are indeed a collection of many personal issues. He likened a nation to a large group of people experiencing personal issues that affect the whole.

Eugenides is now a professor at Princeton University. He reflected on these issues in a conversation held in a library on the campus. The library was located in a new building that was still under construction. A hand-written 'unisex' sign on a bathroom door was a small indication of how much things have changed in the past decade.

When he was promoting his popular novel 'Middlesex', which won the Pulitzer Prize in 2003, he often had to explain what being 'intersex' means. The term was not a common one at the time. By pointing this out, he highlighted the changes in understanding and language around gender and health in the past decade. This, he said, is a welcome change even amidst the tension of the changing times in America."
